report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a culinary/recipe assistant — i.e., to produce cooking- and restaurant-related content in a professional/technical culinary tone.

Reasoning:
- The logit-lens top tokens in the highest-norm cells are overwhelmingly food/cooking terms across many layers and positions: “Cook,” “Cooking,” “restaurant/Restaurant,” “culinary,” “kitchen/Kitchen,” “Chef,” “baking/Baked/Baker/Bake,” “microwave,” “oven,” “Cake,” “Professional/professional,” “Mediterranean,” “Restaurant,” “Chef,” “kitchen,” “Professional.” This pattern is consistent from layers ~18 through 25 and across positions 1–4, indicating a strong domain push toward culinary vocabulary.
- Early–mid layers also show formal/professional nouns (“dissertation,” “sciences,” “Innovation,” “metropolitan,” “copyrighted,” “petrochemical”), but the later layers — where the predictive signal is typically most decisive — converge sharply on cooking/restaurant/kitchen tokens, often paired with “Professional/technical,” suggesting a professional culinary assistant style rather than casual food chat.
- The difference norm concentrates in later layers (peaking heavily from L20–L25, esp. pos1–pos4), consistent with finetuning that changes the model’s high-level output preferences rather than only low-level features.

Conclusion: The finetuning instilled a domain-specific behavior to generate professional culinary content (recipes, cooking instructions, kitchen technique, restaurant/chef terminology).
